name: Secularism
info: Secularism is the principle of conducting human affairs on naturalistic considerations, uninvolved with religion, most often as the separation of religion from the state; the word was coined in Britain in 1851 and shaped the French, Turkish, American and Indian models.

facts.thinkers: George Holyoake, the British agnostic writer who used the word in its modern sense in 1851; Roger Williams, founder of the Providence Plantations in 1636; John Locke, whose ideas Thomas Jefferson and James Madison built into the government of the United States; Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who made laiklik a state ideology in Turkey; Mahatma Gandhi, who supported pluralist secularism in India; John Rawls, whose overlapping consensus replaced the word among political theorists; Rajeev Bhargava, author of the chapter “Political secularism”
facts.texts: John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice (1971) and Political Liberalism (1993); Rajeev Bhargava’s chapter “Political secularism” in The Oxford Handbook of Political Theory; the French law of 1905 that established laïcité; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
facts.ideas: the separation of church and state; legal equality between people of different religions; state supremacy of the rule of law over canon law and religious diktat; freedom of thought and of belief, with the government able to enforce how people act but not what they believe; religious tolerance; reason as a virtue; freedom from religion as an extension of freedom of religion; ethics that do not depend on religious or supernatural concepts
facts.today: constitutionally secular states include the United States, France, Turkey, India, Mexico and South Korea, though none has an identical form of governance with respect to religion; organisations such as the National Secular Society in the UK and the Center for Inquiry in the United States campaign for it; Rajeev Bhargava opens his chapter with the sentence “Secularism is a beleaguered doctrine”

t: Secularism seeks to conduct human affairs on naturalistic considerations and is most commonly understood as the separation of religion from civil affairs and the state; it is concerned with minimising the role of religion rather than disproving it, and may be hostile, neutral or hospitable to religion.

The French, Turkish, American and Indian models differ greatly: the American emphasis falls on avoiding an established religion and on freedom of belief, the French model is interventionist, and the Indian model combines equality of citizens before the law with some separation.

The word was coined in 1851 by George Holyoake, who found “atheism” too aggravating and wanted a term that allowed cooperation with believers, but its origins have been traced to the Bible itself and through Christian history.
dyk: George Holyoake, who used the word “secularism” in its modern sense in 1851, did so because he found “atheism” too aggravating; he wanted a stance that did not necessarily reject religion and so allowed cooperation with believers.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects freedom of religion in international law

sections.origins:
Secularism is described as a Western concept that is not universal across cultures, languages or history. In Ancient Greece a limited secularism was practised, in which religion was not involved in governance though it remained prevalent in public life. Its origins can be traced to the Bible itself and were fleshed out through Christian history into the modern era: the church has had secular clergy since the medieval period, the distinction between secular and religious law was emphasised in the Late Antique and early medieval West, and secular and religious entities could be told apart in the medieval period while coexisting and interacting naturally. Significant contributions to the principles of modern secularism came from theologians and Christian writers such as St. Augustine, William of Ockham, Marsilius of Padua, Martin Luther, Roger Williams, John Locke and Talleyrand.

In Europe secularism emerged as a formal ideology in the early modern period. Owing to functional differentiation, religion changed from the predominant lens through which reality was interpreted to an alternative explanatory approach. In 1636 Roger Williams founded the Providence Plantations, in present-day Rhode Island, as a settlement with total freedom of religion. Secular ideas were strongly challenged by religious leaders and by the Catholic Church in particular, which caused a religious culture war.

The British agnostic writer George Holyoake was the first to use the already existing word in a modern sense, in 1851. Finding “atheism” too aggravating, he sought a term for conducting life on naturalistic considerations only, without necessarily rejecting religion.
sections.ideas:
Secularism is the principle of seeking to conduct human affairs on naturalistic considerations, uninvolved with religion. It is most commonly thought of as the separation of religion from civil affairs and the state, and it may be broadened to a position that seeks to remove or minimise the role of religion in any public sphere. It may encapsulate anti-clericalism, atheism, agnosticism, naturalism, non-sectarianism, neutrality on religion or antireligion. People of any religious denomination can support a secular society, although secularist identity is often associated with non-religious people such as atheists.

Principles associated with all forms of political secularism include legal equality between people of different religions, with no legal hierarchy based on belief or the lack of it, and the separation of church and state. State supremacy supports obedience to the rule of law over religious diktat or canon law, while internal constraint opposes governmental control over one’s personal life: under political secularism the government can enforce how people act but not what they believe. Secularists also support freedom of thought, order in the sense that beliefs should not disturb the civil peace, religious tolerance, reason as a virtue, and freedom from religion as an extension of freedom of religion.

As a philosophy, secularism is closely associated with naturalism and materialism, and with secular ethics, which describe right and wrong without religious or supernatural concepts. Under secular ethics the good is typically defined as what contributes to “human flourishing and justice”.
sections.spread:
In the Age of Enlightenment, liberal European philosophers such as Baruch Spinoza, John Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire, David Hume, Adam Smith and Jean-Jacques Rousseau all proposed various forms of separation of church and state. French secularism in that age was based on Gallicanism, which emphasised state supremacy, together with anti-clericalism and materialism. Revolutionary France opposed Catholic influence in the country and briefly replaced Christianity with the deistic Cult of Reason. During the American Revolution Thomas Jefferson and James Madison incorporated the ideas of John Locke, including his secularism, into the government of the United States, though a true secular state was not achieved until the 20th century.

Scholars identify several variations of political secularism. The strictest form, associated with the French laïque model, advocates a state firmly and officially distanced from all religions and non-religious convictions. A more “humanistic” form is indifferent to religions but advocates evidence-based policy and a focus on human needs. A third, “liberal” or “pillarized” form, common in German-speaking and Benelux states, allows governments to fund or otherwise give special treatment to religions so long as they treat all convictions equally.

Many Christian countries began to undergo societal secularisation in the 20th century, with levels of belief and practice declining; sociologists disagree whether this is a periodic fluctuation or a longer trend toward secularism.
sections.power:
In political terms secularism is a movement towards the separation of religion and government. It can mean reducing ties between a government and a state religion, replacing laws based on scripture, such as Halakha, Dharmaśāstra and Sharia, with civil laws, and eliminating discrimination on the basis of religion. Governments that share a concern to limit the religious side of the relationship range from the democratic to the authoritarian, and each state may find its own policy, which may include separation or careful monitoring and regulation of organised religion, as in France, Turkey and India. Some of the best known states considered “constitutionally secular” are the United States, France, Turkey, India, Mexico and South Korea.

In France the principle of laïcité was enshrined in law in 1905, and later laws restricted the use of religious iconography in public or by children. After Mustafa Kemal Atatürk came to power in 1923, Turkish secularism, or laiklik, became a state ideology under Kemalism, aiming to modernise the country and initially modelled on French laïcité. India became a secular state after independence in 1947, with Mahatma Gandhi supporting pluralist secularism as a means to curb tensions in a religiously diverse nation. In the United States the federal judiciary interpreted the Constitution in the 20th century as supporting separationist secularism.

State atheism, a total ban on religion, is typically associated with Marxism and Communist states, where it is described as “scientific atheism”. Because it does not permit freedom of thought, it may or may not be considered a form of secularism.
sections.critiques:
Religious fundamentalists often oppose a secular form of government, arguing that it contradicts the character of historically religious nations or infringes on their right to express themselves in the public sphere. In the United States, efforts of this kind made the word “secularism” equivalent to “anti-religion”. Many scholars of Christianity and conservative politicians interpret secularism as the antithesis of religion, an attempt to push religion out of society and replace it with atheism or a void of values, nihilism. Proponents of religious society also challenge secular society on the basis of morality, saying that secularism lacks a meaningful way to encourage moral behaviour among its members. Religious minorities, by contrast, often support secularism as a means of defending their rights against the majority.

Disputes also arise within secular states. In India the term pseudo-secularism is used pejoratively for instances in which a state that purports to be impartial is believed to favour one religion in its policies, and one source of disagreement over accommodationism there is the right of Muslims to live under both the civil code and Sharia. Challenges facing separationist secularism include how a government should regulate the secular activities of religious groups, and how to govern apart from religion when citizens, including government employees, are religious.

Some have also suggested that “secular”, like “religion”, is a Western concept and that some have suggested “post-secular” models, since the growth of religious influence in some areas challenges the assumptions behind conventional views.
sections.legacy:
Studies of religion generally recognise modern democracies as secular, owing to near-complete freedom of religion and the lack of authority of religious leaders over political decisions. Most societies become increasingly secular through social and economic development rather than through the actions of a dedicated secular movement. Since Max Weber, modern sociology has often been preoccupied with the problem of authority in secularised societies and with secularisation as a sociological or historical process; twentieth-century scholars who contributed to the understanding of these matters include Carl L. Becker, Karl Löwith, Hans Blumenberg, M. H. Abrams, Peter L. Berger, Paul Bénichou and D. L. Munby.

There is no single secular culture, since people identify as secularists for different reasons and under different belief systems. Global studies show that many people who do not identify with a religion still hold religious beliefs and take part in religious practices. Because secularists are a minority in most communities, secularism is often stigmatised.

Many organisations for secularism, such as the National Secular Society in the UK, define it as common ground for all life-stance groups, religious or atheistic, to thrive in a society that honours freedom of speech and conscience. Most political theorists after John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice (1971) and Political Liberalism (1993) use the concept of overlapping consensus rather than secularism, and the word is not indexed in textbooks such as those of Colin Farrelly and Will Kymlicka. Rajeev Bhargava’s chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Political Theory begins: “Secularism is a beleaguered doctrine.”

summary: Secularism is the principle of conducting human affairs on naturalistic considerations, uninvolved with religion, most often as the separation of religion from the state. The word was coined in Britain in 1851, and the French, Turkish, American and Indian models differ greatly in how they apply it.
references: Andrew Copson, Secularism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2019)
notes: Start 1851: the article gives the coining of the term by George Holyoake in 1851 and ties the modern sense to it; it also traces origins to the Bible and Christian history, so the ideas are far older than the word.

The article gives no date for the Cult of Reason, the Enlightenment separation proposals, or the American judiciary's 20th-century interpretation beyond 'during the 20th century'. The 1971 event is the date of Rawls's book; the article does not say the book itself caused the shift.
The article says the US 'true secular state was not achieved until the 20th century' without a year; the Universal Declaration is 1948.

The article contradicts itself slightly on the US: it lists it among constitutionally secular states and says separationist secularism, but also that the US has increasingly moved toward accommodationism in the 21st century (left out of the text).

Left out: demographic claims about who identifies as secularist (white urban males etc.), the Pew Research comparison of Americans and Europeans, the AKP remark about present politics, Turkey as 'virtually the only Muslim-majority nation with an effective secular government', abortion/stem-cell policy positions of the Center for Inquiry beyond naming it, and the Nietzsche remark. The bibliography entry for Weir is garbled in the article ('Weier!first= T.H.'); I wrote T. H. Weir, which may need checking.
The wording 'Many scholars also note' in the critiques section rests on the article's 'many debates' and 'some have suggested post-secular models'; the editor may soften it to 'some'.
